Capability Self-Assessment in Large Language Models

Haoyan Yang ††thanks: Equal Contributions. Affiliation: Stony Brook University    Reza Shirkavand11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Maryland    Yukai Jin Affiliation: Florida State University    Jiawei Zhou ††thanks: Correspondence to: Jiawei Zhou (jiawei.zhou.1@stonybrook.edu), Shangqian Gao (sgao@cs.fsu.edu), Heng Huang (heng@cs.umd.edu). Affiliation: Stony Brook University    Shangqian Gao22 2 We train for 1 epoch on Math and 3 epochs on Science. Affiliation: Florida State University    Heng Huang22 2 We train for 1 epoch on Math and 3 epochs on Science. Affiliation: University of Maryland
Abstract

The ability to recognize one’s own limitations and decide whether to solve a problem or seek help is fundamental to reliable intelligent systems. Yet modern large language models tend to overestimate their competence and attempt queries they cannot solve. We study how models can learn Capability Self-Assessment (CSA) while preserving their problem-solving ability. Because the same model both assesses and solves queries, self-assessment training can change the capability it must recognize. We systematically compare supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), evaluating each trained model’s self-assessment against its updated capability and measuring how well it retains its solving ability. Across model families, scales, and domains, RL provides the strongest assessment–retention trade-off. We also find that CSA transfers to the out-of-distribution settings we evaluate, and demonstrate its practical value for local–cloud routing at inference time and targeted data selection during training. Code is available at https://github.com/Joyyang158/llm-csa.

1 Introduction

An ideal intelligent system not only solves problems well, but also recognizes its limits. It asks for help when a problem exceeds its ability or uses failure to identify what it should learn next, as humans do (Madras et al., 2018). However, large language models (LLMs) often elect to answer queries they cannot solve reliably, leading to hallucinated outputs (Farquhar et al., 2024) and wasted compute (Shirkavand et al., 2025). Prior work has studied whether LLMs can assess answer correctness and recognize unanswerable questions (Kadavath et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2023), and trained models to estimate confidence (Kapoor et al., 2024) or abstain when uncertain (Zhang et al., 2024).

We ask whether a generative model can be post-trained to predict its own query-level success, while preserving its problem-solving ability. We use Capability Self-Assessment (CSA) to denote a pre-answer choice between Self-SOLVE, where the model attempts the query itself, and DELEGATE, where the query is handed to a stronger system. Because the same model both assesses and solves queries, self-assessment training can shift the capability boundary it must recognize. We therefore study how to learn and evaluate model-specific self-assessment policies while accounting for changes in problem-solving ability.

To investigate this question, we compare supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). We evaluate both approaches within a common CSA framework, measuring self-assessment quality alongside changes in the model’s original capabilities. Across model families, scales, and domains, we find that SFT can improve self-assessment at the expense of task performance, whereas RLVR can improve CSA while preserving the model’s problem-solving ability. We observe transfer across domains and datasets, suggesting that the learned assessment policy remains useful beyond its training distribution.

We then explore two practical uses of this learned decision signal. At inference time, CSA improves local–cloud routing by identifying queries that require a stronger model. During training, CSA can be used to identify examples that may lie near or beyond the model’s current competence, providing a targeted signal for data selection. In this way, learned CSA can play a dual role analogous to competence assessment in effective problem solving, guiding when to act or delegate at inference time, and guiding what to learn next during training.

In summary, our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    We evaluate pre-answer capability assessment jointly with the effects of assessment training on the model. We use both aggregate task performance and query-level capability stability to distinguish assessment gains from changes in the capability being assessed.

  2. 2.

    We systematically compare training-free methods, SFT, and RLVR for acquiring CSA. Our experiments show that RLVR can improve self-assessment while preserving problem-solving ability, with evidence of transfer across domains and datasets.

  3. 3.

    We demonstrate the practical value of CSA for local–cloud routing and targeted data selection, guiding both when to seek help and what to learn next.

2 Related Work

Pre-answer capability prediction. Kadavath et al. (2022) distinguish assessment of a generated answer through P(True) from prediction of whether a model knows an answer through P(IK). Their learned P(IK) predictor and cross-task evaluations are direct precedents for our setting. Chen et al. (2026) introduce a training-free query-level uncertainty signal and demonstrate adaptive inference, including model cascading. Barkan et al. (2026) study predictions of task success and their relationship to overconfidence and decision making. We build on this literature by comparing assessment-training methods while measuring their effects on the model and evaluating predictions against its post-training capability.

Confidence, abstention, and deferral. Confidence estimation, abstention, and learning to defer provide closely related objectives and decision rules (Madras et al., 2018; Kapoor et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2025). Sampling-based methods estimate uncertainty from multiple generated outputs (Wang et al., 2023; Manakul et al., 2023; Farquhar et al., 2024; Kossen et al., 2024). Gul et al. (2026) and Damani et al. (2026) use RL to train help-seeking and calibrated confidence, but neither extensively evaluates per-query capability retention.

Our experiments compare these signals and training approaches within the assessment–retention setting. Moreover, unlike much prior work that treats self-knowledge as a safeguard against hallucination, using confidence or abstention to avoid unreliable answers, we explore the model’s own capability boundary as a signal for adaptation. The same learned decision determines when the model acts or seeks help at inference time and which examples it learns from during training. Table 1 provides a comparison of our work and existing studies. Appendix A provides a broader discussion.

3 CSA through Training

Our prompt-only study shows that prompting alone does not elicit reliable CSA in the evaluated settings (Appendix D.1). We therefore compare training strategies for improving this assessment. We formulate CSA learning as policy optimization with a capability-preservation goal and evaluate how well different training methods meet it.

3.1 CSA Formulation

Given a query qiq_{i}, a model makes a binary decision between Self-SOLVE and DELEGATE before attempting an answer. Let yiy_{i} denote its capability label under a specified task and evaluation protocol. The policy πθCSA\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{CSA}} takes xi=[p;qi]x_{i}=[p;q_{i}] as input, where pp is a CSA instruction, and predicts a decision y^i\hat{y}_{i} without observing a candidate solution.

We formulate CSA learning as improving this decision policy while preserving the model’s underlying problem-solving ability. Let θ0\theta_{0} denote the initial model parameters, Δcap​(θ,θ0)\Delta_{\mathrm{cap}}(\theta,\theta_{0}) measure capability change under the same evaluation protocol, and u⁡(y^i,yi)u(\hat{y}_{i},y_{i}) measure agreement between the predicted decision y^i\hat{y}_{i} and the capability label yiy_{i}. The learning objective is

θ⋆=arg​max𝜃​𝔼qi∼𝒟,y^i∼πθCSA(⋅∣xi)​[u⁡(y^i,yi)]s.t.Δcap​(θ,θ0)≤ε,\theta^{\star}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\;\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}q_{i}\sim\mathcal{D},\,\hat{y}_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{CSA}}(\cdot\mid x_{i})\end{subarray}}\left[u\!\left(\hat{y}_{i},y_{i}\right)\right]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\Delta_{\mathrm{cap}}(\theta,\theta_{0})\leq\varepsilon, (1)

where ε\varepsilon specifies the tolerated capability change. The choice of Δcap\Delta_{\mathrm{cap}} determines whether preservation is assessed through aggregate task performance or finer-grained capability profiles. We use fixed capability labels from the initial model as training targets. Because training may change the capability being assessed, we re-probe each trained model for evaluation and separately compare its solving performance with the initial checkpoint. The preservation constraint expresses the desired learning goal, and our training methods do not explicitly enforce it. Figure 1 summarizes the training and evaluation framework.

3.2 CSA Label Construction

We construct training labels by probing the initial model ℳθ0\mathcal{M}_{\theta_{0}} under a fixed task and evaluation protocol. Given a dataset 𝒟={(qi,ai∗)}i=1N\mathcal{D}=\{(q_{i},a_{i}^{*})\}_{i=1}^{N}, we sample KK solution attempts {a^i(k)}k=1K\{\hat{a}_{i}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K} for each query. Let ci(k)=Correct⁡(a^i(k),ai∗)∈{0,1}c_{i}^{(k)}=\mathrm{Correct}(\hat{a}_{i}^{(k)},a_{i}^{*})\in\{0,1\} indicate whether an attempt passes the task-specific correctness check. We aggregate these outcomes into a binary capability label:

yi={Self-Solve,if ​g​({ci(k)}k=1K)=1,Delegate,otherwise,y_{i}=\begin{cases}\textsc{Self-Solve},&\text{if }g\big(\{c_{i}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}\big)=1,\\ \textsc{Delegate},&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases} (2)

where gg is an aggregation rule, such as any-correct or majority-correct. Thus, yiy_{i} denotes the initial model’s empirical capability label for query qiq_{i} under the chosen sampling and aggregation protocol.

We construct these labels once from the initial model and use them across all training strategies. They provide a common training target, but may no longer describe the model after training. We therefore evaluate each trained policy against freshly probed capability labels and separately measure problem-solving retention.

3.3 CSA Training and Evaluation

We compare two post-training paradigms for learning the CSA policy: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Both use the same fixed initial capability labels and query inputs. Each input combines a CSA prompt pp with the query, xi=[p;qi]x_{i}=[p;q_{i}]. See Appendix E for all details.

Within SFT, we compare three forms of supervision.

(a) SFTLabel (Zhang et al., 2024; Kapoor et al., 2024). The target is the bare capability label, oilabel=yio_{i}^{\text{label}}=y_{i}. The model learns to emit the decision directly.

(b) SFTSelf (Kadavath et al., 2022; Chaudhry et al., 2024). The initial model generates a rationale conditioned on the query input and capability label, riself∼ℳθ0(⋅∣xi,yi)r_{i}^{\text{self}}\sim\mathcal{M}_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{i}). The training target is the rationale followed by the label, oiself=[riself;yi]o_{i}^{\text{self}}=[r_{i}^{\text{self}};y_{i}].

(c) SFTTeacher (Hager et al., 2025). A stronger teacher model generates the rationale under the same conditioning, riteacher∼ℳ∗(⋅∣xi,yi)r_{i}^{\text{teacher}}\sim\mathcal{M}^{*}(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{i}). The training target is oiteacher=[riteacher;yi]o_{i}^{\text{teacher}}=[r_{i}^{\text{teacher}};y_{i}].

All three SFT variants minimize the same negative log-likelihood objective:

ℒSFT(θ)=−∑i=1Nlogpθ(oi|xi),oi∈{oilabel,oiself,oiteacher},\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(\theta)=-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p_{\theta}\!\left(o_{i}\,\middle|\,x_{i}\right),\qquad o_{i}\in\{o_{i}^{\text{label}},\,o_{i}^{\text{self}},\,o_{i}^{\text{teacher}}\}, (3)

(d) RLVR. RLVR generates a rationale and a decision, oi(g)=[ri(g);y^i(g)]o_{i}^{(g)}=[r_{i}^{(g)};\hat{y}_{i}^{(g)}], and rewards agreement between the decision and the fixed capability label: Ri(g)=+1R_{i}^{(g)}=+1 if y^i(g)=yi\hat{y}_{i}^{(g)}=y_{i}, and −1-1 otherwise. The reward evaluates the CSA decision, not a generated task answer. We optimize this policy using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024).

Training has two stages. Diversity-Filtered Warm-up (DFW) runs GRPO on queries whose initial GG rollouts contain both Self-SOLVE and DELEGATE decisions. Full GRPO training then continues from the warm-up checkpoint on the full dataset. Appendices B and D.2.2 provide more details. Both stages use the following objective:

ℒGRPO(θ;ℬ)=−𝔼xi∼ℬ{oi(g)}∼πθold[1G∑g=1Gmin(ρi(g)(θ)Ai(g),clip(ρi(g)(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)Ai(g))]+βKL[πθ∥πref],\mathcal{L}_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta;\mathcal{B})=-\,\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x_{i}\sim\mathcal{B}\\ \{o_{i}^{(g)}\}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}\end{subarray}}\!\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\min\!\Big(\rho_{i}^{(g)}(\theta)A_{i}^{(g)},\!\mathrm{clip}\!\big(\rho_{i}^{(g)}(\theta),1{-}\epsilon,1{+}\epsilon\big)A_{i}^{(g)}\Big)\right]+\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\!\left[\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}\right], (4)

where ρi(g)​(θ)=πθ​(oi(g)∣xi)/πθold​(oi(g)∣xi)\rho_{i}^{(g)}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(o_{i}^{(g)}\mid x_{i})/\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(o_{i}^{(g)}\mid x_{i}), ϵ\epsilon is the clipping threshold, β\beta is the KL strength, and Ai(g)=(Ri(g)−meang′​Ri(g′))/stdg′​Ri(g′)A_{i}^{(g)}=(R_{i}^{(g)}-\mathrm{mean}_{g^{\prime}}R_{i}^{(g^{\prime})})/\mathrm{std}_{g^{\prime}}R_{i}^{(g^{\prime})}, which is the group-normalized advantage within each rollout group. ℬ\mathcal{B} is a mini-batch from 𝒟div\mathcal{D}_{\text{div}} (Stage 1) or 𝒟\mathcal{D} (Stage 2).

Connection to Eq. 1.

A Lagrangian relaxation of Eq. 1 produces a regularized objective with a capability penalty Δcap​(θ,θ0)\Delta_{\mathrm{cap}}(\theta,\theta_{0}). RLVR (Eq. 4) uses KL regularization as a heuristic approximation to this penalty. SFT (Eq. 3) maximizes target-output likelihood and can optionally include the same KL penalty; we use vanilla SFT by default, following common practice.

Inference and Evaluation.

At inference time, the trained model receives [p;q][p;q] and outputs a CSA decision, preceded by a rationale for all methods except SFTLabel. We re-probe each trained model on the evaluation queries using the sampling protocol and aggregation rule in Eq. (2), obtaining updated capability labels {y~i}\{\tilde{y}_{i}\}. We measure CSA quality by comparing the predicted decisions y^i\hat{y}_{i} with these labels. Separately, we assess capability retention by comparing task performance before and after training.

4 Experiments and Analysis

4.1 Setup

We conduct experiments on the Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025) family (1.7B, 4B, 8B, 14B), as well as OLMo2 (OLMo et al., 2024) (7B, 13B). Evaluation spans two domains: Math (GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2023), and AIME (Veeraboina, 2024)) and Science (MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024) across the biology, chemistry, health, and physics categories). We use Macro F1 (M-F1) as the primary metric of CSA quality and report Capability Discrimination Score (CDS) as an auxiliary metric. We use Capability Ratio (CR) to measure average retention of the model’s problem-solving ability. Full experimental details appear in Appendix C.

4.2 Main Results

For each query, we instantiate Eq. (2) with K=5K=5 independently sampled task answers. Repeated attempts reduce reliance on a single stochastic outcome. We use any-correct for open-ended Math: at least one answer must be correct. For multiple-choice Science, we use majority-correct: at least three answers must be correct, since guessing an option is more likely to succeed. These labels define capability under the sampling protocol, rather than single-attempt accuracy. Appendix C.1.4 explains the construction, and Appendix D.2.1 varies KK and the aggregation threshold at K=5K=5.

RLVR outperforms SFT in balancing assessment quality and capability retention.

Table 2 shows that, across the evaluated models and tasks, RLVR outperforms the SFT baselines in terms of M-F1 in most cases. It also retains approximately 100% of the original task performance on average. Mean CR is 100.8% on Math and 102.0% on Science, compared with only 33.7% and 19.9% for SFTLabel. The rationale-based SFTSelf and SFTTeacher retain 82.6–90.5% on average across methods and domains. Appendix D.3 illustrates this with training dynamics on Qwen3-4B Science, where RLVR’s CSA predictions remain aligned with its current problem-solving ability, whereas SFTLabel increasingly fits the original labels despite its declining ability.

Furthermore, Table 3 shows that this advantage persists when supervised training is modified to preserve capability, using LoRA, KL regularization, and task mixing. RLVR achieves the highest M-F1 for both model sizes on Math. The results suggest that RLVR’s advantage is not solely attributable to the capability loss induced by standard SFT. See Appendix D.4 for more details.

A closer look at individual decisions helps explain this remaining advantage. SFT can closely match the overall self-solve rate without accurately identifying which queries the model can solve. In Figure 2, SFTTeacher predicts a Self-SOLVE rate of 82.4%, close to its true rate of 81.8%, yet decision accuracy is only 79.0% for SFTTeacher and 76.3% for SFTSelf, compared with 87.8% for RLVR. A policy can match the overall rate yet choose the wrong queries to solve or delegate. RLVR’s higher decision accuracy indicates better discrimination between these queries, beyond matching how often to self-solve.

RLVR vs. training-free baselines.

In Figure 3, CSA-based RLVR outperforms both training-free query-based methods and methods that require generated answers on Qwen3-4B Math. It achieves M-F1 of 0.80, compared with at most 0.57 for query-based baselines, 0.76 for minimum token probability from one answer, and 0.78 and 0.75 for self-consistency and semantic entropy using five answers. Appendix D.5 provides the full baseline setup and more experimental results. Compared with competitive answer-based methods, CSA avoids generating full task solutions before deciding whether to solve or delegate, using about 151 rationale and decision tokens per query in this setting (Appendix D.6). A decision-first format can further reduce token use by stopping as soon as the Self-SOLVE or DELEGATE decision is emitted. Appendix D.2.3 compares this format with analysis-first output across three settings and finds similar CSA performance.

4.3 Capability Retention Analysis

Why retention matters. We could assess the solver with a separate adapter or probe, leaving its solving ability untouched. But these methods are less accurate: they score 0.62–0.73 M-F1 on Math and 0.51–0.56 on Science, versus 0.84–0.85 and 0.66–0.67 for RLVR (Tables 3 and  15). LoRA SFT also performs worse than full-parameter SFT in three of four settings, suggesting insufficient capacity for this task. The best assessment in our experiments comes from changing the solver’s own weights, so preserving its solving ability matters. This also fits practical efficiency, where one updated checkpoint handles both solving and assessment. See Appendix D.4 for more.

The CR results in Tables 2 and 3 show that RLVR largely preserves aggregate task performance, but this can hide changes in which individual queries the model can solve. We therefore compare query-level capability before and after CSA training across eight mathematics and coding settings. As shown in Figure 4, on average 4.5% of capability labels change, compared with 5.4% disagreement expected from repeated finite-sample measurements of the same capability. Agreement between the pre- and post-training labels remains high (κ=0.895\kappa=0.895), while the mean Capability Ratio is 101.0%. These results suggest that CSA training preserves both aggregate performance and the model’s query-level capability boundary within the resolution of our evaluation. Full details are provided in Appendix D.7.

4.4 Generalization of CSA

Within-Source Discrimination

A Math policy could exploit benchmark source identity as a shortcut instead of assessing its ability to solve each query. To test this explanation, we shuffle decisions within GSM8K, MATH500, and AIME while preserving each source’s routing counts and the model’s post-training capability labels. This preserves any advantage from source-level routing but removes the association between individual decisions and query solvability. Figure 6 shows that all six models exceed their null means by 3.44–9.61 M-F1 percentage points. Thus, learned CSA captures query-level differences in solvability within benchmark sources, beyond exploiting benchmark identity. Appendix D.8 gives the experimental protocol and permutation details.

Math–Science Transfer

We assess out-of-distribution generalization by evaluating math-trained policies on science problems and science-trained policies on math problems. Table 4 shows that RLVR achieves the highest M-F1 in three of four cross-domain settings, including both transfer directions for Qwen3-1.7B and Science-to-Math transfer for Qwen3-4B. These results show that its assessment advantage extends beyond the training domain.

Generalization to Omni-MATH

We further evaluate on Omni-MATH (Gao et al., 2025), a held-out mathematics dataset with annotated difficulty levels. Evaluating within a single benchmark lets us examine whether CSA responds to difficulty without relying on differences between benchmark sources. We apply the Qwen3-4B CSA policy trained on Math. Figure 6 shows that its Self-SOLVE rate decreases from 90.7% in the easiest interval to 5.8% in the hardest, with a strong linear association between self-solve rate and difficulty (R2=0.938R^{2}=0.938). The policy also achieves query-level M-F1 of 0.67. Together, these results show that learned CSA transfers to unseen Math queries. It also adjusts its willingness to solve with difficulty while retaining query-level discrimination.

Transfer to Coding

Table 5 tests a larger distribution shift: policies trained only on mathematics or science are evaluated on 722722 Python programming problems. For Qwen3-1.7B, the best transferred policy raises coding-assessment M-F1 from 0.360.36 to 0.640.64. For Qwen3-4B, it rises from 0.410.41 to 0.630.63. Coding ability is preserved, with pass@1 changing from 0.5620.562 to 0.5660.566–0.5780.578 for the 1.7B model and from 0.6750.675 to 0.6760.676 for the 4B model. Together, these results show that CSA transfers to a previously unseen domain and task format. Full details are provided in Appendix D.9.

4.5 CSA Tracks Model-Specific Capability

The alignment between CSA decisions and problem difficulty does not by itself establish model-specific self-assessment. A policy could learn which problems are generally difficult for language models. We test this alternative explanation on 722722 coding problems using OLMoE-1B-7B (Muennighoff et al., 2025) as an independent comparator. For each Qwen policy’s own model and OLMoE, we estimate per-problem competence in the same way by sampling K=32K=32 solutions.

Table 6 shows that CSA decisions track the policy model’s own competence more strongly than OLMoE’s competence. After controlling for OLMoE’s pass rate, the partial correlation between the CSA decision and the policy model’s own pass rate ranges from 0.2240.224 to 0.3220.322. In the reverse direction, after controlling for the policy model’s own pass rate, the partial correlation with OLMoE ranges from only 0.0420.042 to 0.0930.093.

We also construct an OLMoE-based difficulty rule that delegates exactly as many problems as each CSA policy, selecting those with the lowest OLMoE pass rates. CSA achieves 0.050.05–0.060.06 higher Macro-F1 than this rule across all four settings, even though CSA observes only the problem text while the OLMoE rule uses 3232 executed solutions per problem. Thus, the learned policy captures information about which problems its own model can solve beyond a generic estimate of problem difficulty.

Cross-scale policy swapping provides a complementary test. A policy trained for Qwen3-1.7B nearly matches that solver’s aggregate capability, with a coverage–accuracy gap of +0.003+0.003, whereas attaching a policy trained for the stronger Qwen3-8B model to the 1.7B solver produces an +0.110+0.110 gap. Across all pairings, policies matched to their solver have a smaller mean absolute coverage–accuracy gap than mismatched policies (0.0490.049 versus 0.0720.072). While these cross-scale results describe aggregate alignment, the query-level comparisons provide more direct evidence of model-specific assessment. Full results are reported in Appendix D.10.

4.6 Applications

4.6.1 Self-Routing

A model with accurate CSA is a natural router in a local–cloud inference system. When the local model chooses to self-solve, the query is answered on-device. When it chooses to delegate, the query is routed to a powerful cloud model. The local model serves as its own router, offering a practical cost–accuracy trade-off between local-only and cloud-only inference. Table 8 presents the Math routing results using Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B as local models and Qwen3-235B-A22B as the cloud model. Accuracy. CSA routing reaches 0.73 and 0.80 accuracy for the 1.7B and 4B models, outperforming local-only and vanilla routing and improving over random routing by about 8.2 percentage points at matched cloud-call budgets. Efficiency. CSA routing is fast, taking an average of 0.53 seconds per query for Qwen3-1.7B and 0.39 seconds for Qwen3-4B. This enables prompt selection between local answering and cloud delegation with little delay from the routing decision. Appendix D.12.1 provides a detailed illustration and evaluation setup. Appendix D.12.2 further studies single-attempt routing with an expected-outcome reward that accounts for both answer accuracy and delegation cost.

4.6.2 Self-Guided Data Selection

We further test whether CSA can serve as a data-selection signal. Starting from a base model M0M_{0}, we train an RL-based CSA model MRLVRM_{\mathrm{RLVR}} on MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024) and apply it to a fresh candidate pool from MedMCQA (Pal et al., 2022). We select examples based on a metric which prioritizes examples that the CSA model is likely to Delegate while filtering for cases that are uncertain but not extreme loss outliers, and fine-tune the model on this subset. We then compare against standard selection baselines, including random, loss-based, and dev-similarity selection, to assess whether CSA identifies examples that more effectively improve the model’s downstream performance.

Table 8 shows that CSA-based selection generally outperforms the baselines across model sizes and selection budgets. For Qwen3-1.7B, CSA selection improves over the eval-only model at every budget and slightly exceeds training on the full 50K candidate pool when using only 10–20% of the data. The gains are especially pronounced for Qwen3-4B. CSA-selected subsets achieve 55.8–57.4% accuracy, substantially outperforming both the eval-only baseline (42.2%) and training on all examples (47.6%). In contrast, high-loss selection performs poorly across all settings, indicating that simply selecting the hardest examples is not sufficient and can over-emphasize noisy or unlearnable samples. Low-loss selection is the strongest baseline for Qwen3-4B, but remains well below CSA-based selection. These results suggest that the learned CSA signal identifies examples that are not merely difficult or similar to the development set, but are especially useful for improving the model under a limited fine-tuning budget. See Appendix D.12.3 for the full details.

5 Conclusion

We studied how LLMs can acquire CSA while retaining the solving ability being assessed. Through a systematic study, we showed RLVR training provides the strongest overall assessment–retention trade-off among the evaluated training strategies. We also demonstrated out-of-distribution generalization of CSA. More broadly, CSA shifts self-knowledge from a safeguard against errors to a signal for adaptation, guiding both when a model acts and what it learns next. We believe CSA is a promising building block for more adaptive, trustworthy, and responsible AI systems. Ultimately, intelligence is not only about solving problems, but also about recognizing the limits of one’s own competence, and adapting when needed.
