Appendix A Related Work

Our work draws on research on self-evaluation and calibration, selective prediction and abstention, uncertainty estimation, learning to defer, and decision-making with external tools. These areas have shown that LLMs can expose useful signals about correctness and answerability and can use such signals to abstain or seek assistance. We focus on a particular coupling within this broader literature: the same generative model is trained to assess its own query-level success before answering, even though this training may alter the capability being assessed. We therefore study self-assessment quality together with capability retention and evaluate whether the resulting behavior transfers beyond its training distribution.

A.1 Self-Evaluation and Calibration of Correctness in LLMs

Kadavath et al. (2022) study whether models can estimate the correctness of their own outputs through quantities such as P(True) and P(IK). That work shows that larger models can exhibit useful self-evaluation signals when queried in the right format, and it helped establish a widely used framing of LLM self-knowledge as a calibration (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007; Guo et al., 2017) problem. Follow-up work has stressed both the promise and limits of this perspective. Yin et al. (2023) ask whether LLMs know what they do not know, focusing on unanswerable questions and explicit uncertainty recognition, while Kapoor et al. (2024) argue that prompting alone is not enough and show that uncertainty estimation benefits substantially from explicit fine-tuning. Zhang et al. (2024) show models can be instruction-tuned to say I don’t know. Barkan et al. (2026) study whether LLMs can predict their own task success and find all tested LLMs are overconfident. Damani et al. (2026) jointly train for answer correctness and calibrated confidence. Together, these studies show that uncertainty awareness is partly learnable and can be expressed through scores, verbal judgments, or abstention behavior.

A large practical literature studies how to extract usable confidence from aligned systems (Chuang et al., 2025). Tian et al. (2023) show that for RLHF-tuned models, verbalized confidences (numbers or linguistic markers produced as tokens) can be more calibrated than raw conditional probabilities on several QA benchmarks, and they catalog prompting/temperature-scaling strategies for eliciting confidence. Mielke et al. (2022) propose linguistic calibration for dialogue agents to better align the style of uncertainty expression with correctness, highlighting that calibration is not only numeric but also communicative.

A parallel line scrutinizes verbalized uncertainty and its failure modes. Sun et al. (2025) find five LLMs overestimate the probability that their answer is correct by 20–60% on reasoning problems. Chhikara (2025) analyze overconfidence as mismatch between predicted confidence and true correctness across QA datasets. Xiong et al. (2023) show that LLMs can be systematically overconfident when asked to verbalize confidence, though calibration and error prediction improve with scale and with specific elicitation strategies (e.g., consistency-based approaches). Groot & Valdenegro-Toro (2024) further evaluate verbalized uncertainty across LLMs/VLMs and emphasize overconfidence as a recurring concern. Yang et al. (2024a) synthesize why empirical findings about verbalized confidence disagree across papers (prompting styles, evaluation setups), reinforcing the need for decision-centric evaluation rather than relying on any single elicitation recipe.

These methods provide natural signals and baselines for CSA, since confidence estimates can be converted into answer-or-abstain decisions through thresholding. Our focus is therefore not a categorical distinction between scores and policies, but the shared-parameter setting in which the same model learns a pre-answer, model-specific decision while retaining the problem-solving ability being assessed. Cross-domain evaluation tests whether this behavior extends beyond its training distribution.

A.2 Selective Prediction, Abstention, and Risk-Coverage Evaluation

The classical foundation for abstention (Ziyin et al., 2019) is the reject option, often traced to Chow (1970), who derives optimal decision rules trading misclassification error against rejection cost. Modern selective prediction (El-Yaniv & Wiener, 2010) formalizes this as optimizing a risk–coverage trade-off—achieving low error on the subset of instances the model elects to answer.

In deep learning, Geifman & El-Yaniv (2019) treat selective classification as choosing a subset to minimize selective risk subject to a coverage constraint. The broader “learning with rejection” literature develops surrogate losses and theoretical analyses for reject option learning (Bartlett & Wegkamp, 2008).

Within NLP specifically, Xin et al. (2021) revisit selective prediction for language tasks, comparing confidence estimators and introducing regularization tricks to improve confidence without heavy compute. Gu & Hopkins (2023) provide a methodological audit of selective prediction evaluation in NLP and propose additional metrics (e.g., refinement) to separate the quality of confidence scores from downstream accuracy.

For LLMs, a current synthesis is Wen et al. (2025), which organizes abstention methods by lifecycle stage (pretraining, alignment (Yang et al., 2024b), inference), and emphasizes that abstention must be evaluated not only technically but also relative to user values and deployment context.

A.3 Hallucination Detection

Hallucination detection addresses related failures in which a model produces unsupported or incorrect content, sometimes with unwarranted confidence (Ji et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2024; Gekhman et al., 2024). A prominent black-box detection approach is SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al., 2023) which detects hallucinated sentences by sampling multiple outputs and measuring disagreement/contradiction—motivated by the intuition that knowledgeable generations are more self-consistent. A complementary statistically grounded approach is semantic entropy: Farquhar et al. (2024) propose uncertainty estimators at the level of meaning, showing that entropy over semantic equivalence classes can detect a subset of hallucinations (confabulations) and generalize to unseen questions. Kossen et al. (2024) then introduce semantic entropy probes designed to make such uncertainty signals cheaper while retaining detection quality.

Internal representations can carry correctness/answerability signals even when outputs are overconfident (Binder et al., 2025). Azaria & Mitchell (2023) show that linear classifiers on hidden states can predict statement truthfulness better than sequence probability alone, suggesting that internal representations contain information relevant to output reliability. Slobodkin et al. (2023) focus on unanswerability: they find indications that models encode answerability, even when they still generate hallucinated answers for unanswerable questions. Newer probe-based hallucination detectors (Han et al., 2025) push this toward practical deployment (e.g., linear probes for long-form generation) while reducing the cost relative to multi-sampling. A related direction (Cencerrado et al., 2025) predicts answer correctness from question-only activations, indicating that some correctness signals may be present before decoding the full answer—useful for early deferral/abstention.

A.4 Conformal Prediction and Statistical Risk Control for LLMs

Conformal prediction (CP) methods usually provide post-hoc risk control (thresholding, filtering, prediction sets) rather than directly modifying the LLM’s parameters. CP provides distribution-free coverage guarantees under exchangeability assumptions (Angelopoulos & Bates, 2023; Shafer & Vovk, 2008; Vovk et al., 2005). Because exact conditional coverage is generally impossible in finite samples, modern work develops controlled relaxations and conditional targets; Gibbs et al. (2025) formalize a spectrum between marginal and conditional validity that is useful when risk differs by topic or subgroup.

Several recent works adapt CP to LMs and text. Quach et al. (2023) propose Conformal Language Modeling, producing sets/subsets of outputs (or filtered segments of text) with validity guarantees for language model generations. Kumar et al. (2023) apply conformal prediction to multiple-choice QA with LLMs, arguing CP produces useful uncertainty sets correlated with accuracy. Because many deployed LLMs are API-only, Su et al. (2024) propose CP methods that do not require access to logits, improving applicability in closed models.

For open-ended generation (Campos et al., 2024), correctness-labeling and scoring functions become the bottleneck: CP guarantees depend on a nonconformity score that must detect errors in generated text. Lee et al. (2024) address this by using textual entailment to define correctness of generated sequences and propose selective generation algorithms controlling false discovery rates (FDR) over entailment relations. Cherian et al. (2024) propose enhanced conformal methods for validity guarantees on LLM outputs, explicitly noting issues of topic-dependent reliability and the utility loss from overly aggressive filtering; they propose conditional-conformal-inspired adaptations and methods to improve the scoring function.

A.5 Learning Decision Policies with RL

RL with verifiable rewards can optimize terminal decisions while allowing intermediate reasoning to emerge from interaction with the reward signal (Guo et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024). A broader literature studies tool use and help-seeking through prompting, self-supervised training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning (Yao et al., 2022; Schick et al., 2023; Nakano et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2025; Du et al., 2024; Gul et al., 2026). These methods typically learn whether an external resource improves downstream task utility. Our setting instead isolates prediction of the assessed model’s own success and evaluates how learning this decision affects the model’s underlying problem-solving ability. We use RL as one approach to optimizing this decision and compare it directly with supervised alternatives.

A.6 Data Selection and Curriculum Learning

Albalak et al. (2024) survey data selection for language models across goals such as quality, diversity, difficulty, and efficiency, and highlight that naively training on all available data may be suboptimal or infeasible (Mindermann et al., 2022). A prominent practical method is DoReMi (Xie et al., 2023), which optimizes domain mixture weights via distributionally robust optimization on a proxy model and then scales training on a reweighted mixture, improving efficiency and average downstream performance. More recently, data selection has been formulated as an optimal control problem over training dynamics (Gu et al., 2024), providing language to treat data scheduling as a sequential decision problem. Classical curriculum learning shows that organizing examples by difficulty can improve optimization and generalization (Bengio et al., 2009).

Our application uses CSA scores as a model-specific signal for data selection. Examples receiving stronger delegation scores are likely to be difficult for the current model, while loss-based filtering removes examples that are already too easy or appear excessively difficult or noisy. This connects CSA to difficulty-aware data selection.

A.7 Relation to Adjacent Formulations

Our distinction from related work concerns the joint setting in which the target is the assessed model’s own success and self-assessment training may alter the capability being assessed. Moreover, unlike much prior work that treats self-knowledge as a safeguard against hallucination, using confidence or abstention to avoid unreliable answers, we explore the model’s own capability boundary as a signal for adaptation. The same learned decision determines when the model acts or seeks help at inference time and which examples it learns from during training.

Appendix B RLVR Training Algorithm

We provide details and pseudocode for the two-stage GRPO procedure summarized in Section 3.3. The binary reward is +1+1 when a rollout predicts the ground-truth CSA label and −1-1 otherwise. Prompted base models often predict Self-SOLVE on nearly every query (Appendix D.1). Applying GRPO directly can therefore yield rollout groups with a single label, vanishing reward variance, and no useful policy-gradient signal.

Stage 1: Diversity-Filtered Warm-up (DFW).

We construct a fixed diversified subset 𝒟div⊆𝒟\mathcal{D}_{\text{div}}\subseteq\mathcal{D} by retaining only queries whose GG rollouts from the initial policy πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} contain both Self-SOLVE and DELEGATE. Under our decision reward, these screening groups contain both reward values. We then run TwarmT_{\text{warm}} GRPO steps on fresh rollouts from 𝒟div\mathcal{D}_{\text{div}}, concentrating early training on queries that exhibited decision diversity and producing checkpoint θwarm\theta_{\text{warm}}.

DFW is related to DAPO’s dynamic sampling (Yu et al., 2025), which filters uniformly rewarded rollout groups while constructing training batches. Both use within-query reward variation to identify useful training opportunities. DFW instead selects a fixed query subset using the initial policy, trains on fresh rollouts from that subset for a limited warm-up period, and then returns to the full dataset.

Stage 2: Full GRPO Training.

Starting from θwarm\theta_{\text{warm}}, we train for another TfullT_{\text{full}} steps on the full dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, where the now-informative advantages drive learning across both solvable and unsolvable queries. Algorithm 1 gives the complete procedure.

Appendix C Experimental Setup

C.1 Main Experimental Setup

C.1.1 Models

Our prompt-only CSA evaluation (Appendix D.1) spans the Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), Gemma3 (Gemma Team and others, 2025), Llama3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), OLMo2 (OLMo et al., 2024), GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025), and Gemini 3.1 (Google DeepMind, 2026) families, covering both open-weight and frontier closed-weight models.

For CSA through training experiments, we experiment with two model families. From the Qwen3 family (Yang et al., 2025), we use four scales: 1.7B, 4B, 8B, and 14B parameters, to study how CSA varies with model capacity within a single family. We additionally include OLMo2 (OLMo et al., 2024) at 7B and 13B parameters to assess generalization across model families. For the SFT Teacher strategy, we use Qwen3-235B-A22B as the teacher model.

C.1.2 Datasets

We evaluate on two domains: Math and Science. The prompt-only study in Appendix D.1 uses the Math test set. Our main results in Section 4 cover both domains.

Math.

We aggregate problems from three sources spanning a wide difficulty spectrum: GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) (grade-school arithmetic word problems), MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2023) (competition-style problems across algebra, geometry, number theory, etc.), and AIME (Veeraboina, 2024) (American Invitational Mathematics Examination problems from 1983 to 2024). All problems have open-ended numerical or symbolic answers. Table 9(a) summarizes the size of each source and the train/test split used in our experiments.

Science.

We use multiple-choice questions from MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), restricted to four science-relevant categories: biology, chemistry, health, and physics. Each question has about 10 answer options, and we feed the question together with all options as the query to the model. Table 9(b) reports the per-category counts and the overall train/test split.

C.1.3 CSA Inference Setup

We use vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) for inference across all evaluated models. Sampling parameters are kept consistent across models:

  • •

    Temperature: 1.0

  • •

    Top-pp: 1.0

  • •

    Top-kk: -1

  • •

    Number of samples per query: 1

For closed-weight models (GPT-5, Gemini 3.1), we query the official APIs provided by OpenAI and Google.

C.1.4 Label Construction

A single sampled answer can succeed or fail because of decoding variability. We therefore sample KK independent task solutions and aggregate their correctness into a binary capability label. Repeated attempts provide evidence about the model’s ability under a specified sampling protocol, rather than treating one failed generation as proof that the query is unsolvable. We use K=5K=5 to obtain this evidence at a moderate evaluation cost. Increasing KK also changes the meaning of an any-correct label, so KK is part of the target definition rather than only a variance-reduction parameter. Appendix D.2.1 examines other values of KK and aggregation thresholds.

Let ci(k)∈{0,1}c_{i}^{(k)}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether attempt kk answers query ii correctly. We assign Self-SOLVE when the relevant condition below holds, and DELEGATE otherwise.

Math: any-correct.

For open-ended Math, the condition is ∑k=1Kci(k)≥1\sum_{k=1}^{K}c_{i}^{(k)}\geq 1: at least one of the five attempts must be correct. Guessing an exact open-ended answer is generally less likely than guessing a multiple-choice option. A correct attempt therefore provides useful evidence that the model can solve the problem, even if its sampled solutions are not consistently successful. This label measures success within KK attempts, not reliable success on a single attempt. If the single-attempt success probability is pp, independent sampling gives an any-correct probability of 1−(1−p)K1-(1-p)^{K}.

Science: majority-correct.

For multiple-choice Science, we require ∑k=1Kci(k)>K/2\sum_{k=1}^{K}c_{i}^{(k)}>K/2, or at least three correct answers out of five. A single correct option can arise by guessing, so a majority provides stronger evidence of consistent success. We independently shuffle the option order for each attempt to reduce reliance on option position. Neither majority voting nor option shuffling eliminates all chance successes; the rule makes the target more stringent than any-correct for this answer format.

Training labels are constructed from the initial model and held fixed. For evaluation, we repeat the same procedure with each trained model to assess decisions against its current capability. The single-attempt routing objective is discussed separately in Appendix D.12.2.

C.1.5 Evaluation Metrics

Macro F1 (M-F1).

Our primary assessment metric, M-F1, is the unweighted mean of the per-class F1 scores for the Self-SOLVE and DELEGATE classes,

M−F​1=12​(F1Self-SOLVE+F1DELEGATE),M-F1=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\mathrm{F1}_{\textsc{Self-SOLVE}}+\mathrm{F1}_{\textsc{DELEGATE}}\right), (5)

where each per-class F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall on that class:

F1c=2​Precc⋅ReccPrecc+Recc,c∈{Self-SOLVE,DELEGATE}.\mathrm{F1}_{c}=\frac{2\,\mathrm{Prec}_{c}\cdot\mathrm{Rec}_{c}}{\mathrm{Prec}_{c}+\mathrm{Rec}_{c}},\qquad c\in\{\textsc{Self-SOLVE},\textsc{DELEGATE}\}. (6)

The two classes receive equal weight, so performance on both contributes to the score. Class prevalence and errors on a rare class can still affect M-F1.

Example: on a test set of 100 queries with 60 true Self-SOLVE and 40 true DELEGATE, suppose the model predicts Self-SOLVE on 70 queries (50 correct, 20 false) and DELEGATE on 30 queries (20 correct, 10 false). Then PrecSelf-SOLVE=50/70≈0.71\mathrm{Prec}_{\textsc{Self-SOLVE}}=50/70\approx 0.71, RecSelf-SOLVE=50/60≈0.83\mathrm{Rec}_{\textsc{Self-SOLVE}}=50/60\approx 0.83, giving F1Self-SOLVE≈0.77\mathrm{F1}_{\textsc{Self-SOLVE}}\approx 0.77. Similarly, PrecDELEGATE=20/30≈0.67\mathrm{Prec}_{\textsc{DELEGATE}}=20/30\approx 0.67, RecDELEGATE=20/40=0.50\mathrm{Rec}_{\textsc{DELEGATE}}=20/40=0.50, giving F1DELEGATE≈0.57\mathrm{F1}_{\textsc{DELEGATE}}\approx 0.57. Thus M−F​1=12​(0.77+0.57)≈0.67M-F1=\tfrac{1}{2}(0.77+0.57)\approx 0.67.

Capability Discrimination Score (CDS).

We report CDS as an auxiliary measure of the separation in capability-label proportions between queries assigned Self-SOLVE and those assigned DELEGATE. Concretely, we partition the test set by the model’s predicted label and let pSp_{S} and pDp_{D} denote the fractions of queries labeled solvable within the Self-SOLVE and DELEGATE groups, respectively, with group sizes nSn_{S} and nDn_{D}. These fractions use the same K=5K=5 capability labels as M-F1. CDS is the (unpooled) two-proportion zz-statistic

C​D​S=pS−pDpS​(1−pS)nS+pD​(1−pD)nD,CDS=\frac{p_{S}-p_{D}}{\sqrt{\dfrac{p_{S}(1-p_{S})}{n_{S}}+\dfrac{p_{D}(1-p_{D})}{n_{D}}}}, (7)

which normalizes the difference in solvable-label proportions by its estimated standard error. Its magnitude depends on sample size and group balance, and it can be unstable when a group is small or its accuracy is near zero or one. We therefore use M-F1 for our main assessment comparisons and do not interpret CDS as a comparable effect size across datasets.

Example: suppose the policy assigns nS=200n_{S}=200 queries to Self-SOLVE and nD=100n_{D}=100 to DELEGATE. Under the K=5K=5 capability-label protocol, 170 queries in the first group and 20 in the second are labeled solvable. Thus pS=170/200=0.85p_{S}=170/200=0.85 and pD=20/100=0.20p_{D}=20/100=0.20, giving

C​D​S=0.85−0.200.85⋅0.15200+0.20⋅0.80100≈13.7.CDS=\frac{0.85-0.20}{\sqrt{\dfrac{0.85\cdot 0.15}{200}+\dfrac{0.20\cdot 0.80}{100}}}\approx 13.7.
Capability Ratio (CR).

To verify that CSA training preserves the model’s original capabilities, we report CR, defined as the percentage of the original model’s problem-solving accuracy retained after CSA training:

C​R=AccpostAccpre×100%,CR=\frac{\text{Acc}_{\text{post}}}{\text{Acc}_{\text{pre}}}\times 100\%, (8)

where Accpre\text{Acc}_{\text{pre}} and Accpost\text{Acc}_{\text{post}} denote the model’s problem-solving accuracy before and after CSA training, respectively. To reduce variance from stochastic decoding, both Accpre\text{Acc}_{\text{pre}} and Accpost\text{Acc}_{\text{post}} are averaged over 5 independent runs. We compute ratios and aggregate statistics from unrounded values and round only for presentation.

Example: if the model solves 60% of the test queries before CSA training (Accpre=0.60\text{Acc}_{\text{pre}}=0.60) and 57% after (Accpost=0.57\text{Acc}_{\text{post}}=0.57), then C​R=0.57/0.60×100%=95%CR=0.57/0.60\times 100\%=95\%.

C.2 Training Settings

Table 10 reports the hyperparameters for both SFT and GRPO. SFT and GRPO both use full-parameter updates, implemented with the TRL library11 1 https://github.com/huggingface/trl on top of DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 (Rasley et al., 2020).

DFW Hyperparameters.

For DFW training, we use the same hyperparameter setup as in Table 10, except for the number of training steps, which we report in Table 11 for each model. Because the size of the diversified subset varies across models, the training schedule differs accordingly: smaller models yield larger subsets and are typically early-stopped before a full epoch, while larger models, with smaller subsets, are trained for 1–2 epochs. This keeps the total number of training steps roughly comparable across model sizes.

Training Pipeline across Model Families.

Another point worth noting is the difference in training pipelines across model families. For Qwen3 models, we follow the full two-stage RLVR pipeline described in Section 3.3. For OLMo2 models, we omit the DFW stage, since they already produce sufficiently diverse responses during rollout as shown in Table 11. This is consistent with Figure 7 in Appendix D.1: while Qwen3 models exhibit Self-SOLVE rates close to 100%, OLMo2 models show noticeably lower Self-SOLVE rates, indicating greater rollout diversity without explicit intervention.

Hardware.

All main experiments are run on NVIDIA B200 GPUs. SFT runs use a single B200, except for Qwen3-14B and OLMo2-13B, which use 2 ×\times B200s. All GRPO runs use 4 ×\times B200s.

C.3 Capability-Preserving Training Baseline Setup

This experiment extends the main training comparison in Table 2 by testing whether RLVR’s advantage persists when supervised training better preserves capability or uses the same example-selection curriculum. Table 12 summarizes the controls; results appear in Table 3 and Appendix D.4. This is a separate controlled comparison on two model sizes, not a rerun of every cell in Table 2.

C.3.1 Models and data

We compare capability self-assessment methods using Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B, training separate models for math and science. The math dataset contains 2,260 training and 490 test questions from GSM8K, MATH500, and AIME. The science dataset contains 3,266 training and 700 test questions from MMLU-Pro biology, chemistry, health, and physics. For each model and domain, we reserve 300 training questions for validation using a split stratified by the initial model’s correctness label.

We obtain supervision by sampling five task answers per question from the initial model. A math question is labeled solvable if any sample is correct, while a science question is labeled solvable if a majority of five option-shuffled attempts are correct. Solvable and unsolvable questions receive SELF_SOLVE and DELEGATE labels, respectively. For SFT, the teacher model generates one rationale conditioned on each label. All generative methods use an analysis-first response format consisting of an <analysis> block followed by a <decision> block.

C.3.2 Baselines

We include the prompted, untrained model; full-parameter SFT with smaller lr; LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) SFT with rank 16, scaling factor 32, and dropout 0.05 on attention and MLP projections; KL-regularized full SFT with a forward DKL(πinitial∥π)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{initial}}\|\pi) penalty of weight 0.05. We also train an additional SFT baseline with a 1:1 mixture of capability self-assessment examples and task-solving rehearsal examples. Each rehearsal target is the initial model’s shortest correct generation for a training question, paired with the exact prompt that produced it. For science, this preserves the sampled option ordering. The two example types receive equal loss weight. We also compare with SFT with the same example-selection curriculum as DFW RLVR, and a supervised classifier on frozen, question-only model representations.

C.3.3 Optimization and selection

For the generative methods, we use an effective batch size of 64 questions, yielding 31 updates for math and 47 for science. SFT uses completion-only loss and a 4,096-token sequence limit. Training uses four GPUs, bfloat16, AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017), weight decay 0.01, a cosine learning-rate schedule, and 10% warm-up. We select the best config between learning rates of 10−610^{-6} and 10−510^{-5} for full-parameter SFT, 10−610^{-6} and 10−410^{-4} for LoRA SFT, and 10−610^{-6} for RLVR.

Appendix D Additional Results

D.1 Prompt-Only CSA Study

We examine whether prompting alone elicits decisions that reflect a model’s measured ability. Prior work reports overconfidence in verbalized confidence (Xiong et al., 2023) and predictions of task success (Barkan et al., 2026). Here we examine this issue through the Self-SOLVE / DELEGATE decision used in our CSA formulation.

Experimental setup.

We evaluate the Qwen3, Gemma3, Llama3, OLMo2, GPT-5, and Gemini 3.1 families, covering open-weight and closed-weight models at multiple scales (Appendix C.1.1). All models use the same combined Math test set of 490 queries: 300 from GSM8K, 100 from MATH500, and 90 from AIME. Dataset details appear in Appendix C.1.2. No CSA training is applied in this study.

For each query, we prompt the model to assess its own capability and choose Self-SOLVE or DELEGATE before generating a task solution. The prompt requests an analysis followed by a structured decision (Appendix E.1). We obtain one assessment per query. Separately, we measure task accuracy using one solution attempt per query and compare the answer with ground truth. Task accuracy is measured on the full test set, including queries the model chooses to delegate. Open-weight inference uses vLLM, while closed-weight models are accessed through their official APIs. The assessment sampling settings are reported in Appendix C.1.3.

Measurements.

The self-solve rate is the fraction of queries assigned Self-SOLVE. The task accuracy is the fraction answered correctly in the separate solving evaluation. We compare these two rates for each model. This preliminary study uses one task attempt per query. The main training experiments instead construct capability labels from five attempts, as described in Appendix C.1.4.

Results and interpretation.

Figure 7 shows that the self-solve rate exceeds task accuracy for every evaluated model. Under this protocol, models choose to answer more queries than they successfully solve. This pattern is consistent with capability overestimation and extends the prior observations to our explicit decision setting. Some models choose Self-SOLVE on nearly every query, leaving little scope for selective help-seeking.

The gap measures aggregate mismatch, rather than whether the model identifies the right queries to solve or delegate. Matching the two rates alone would not establish accurate self-assessment: a model could select the correct number of queries but select the wrong ones. A single solution attempt also provides a noisy estimate of query-level capability. We therefore use repeated attempts and query-level assessment metrics in the main experiments, alongside capability retention. This study motivates learning CSA beyond the behavior elicited by the evaluated prompt. It does not establish that all prompting strategies fail.

D.2 Ablation Studies

D.2.1 Capability-Label Construction

We examine how the number of samples KK and the aggregation threshold affect Math CSA performance. Results are broadly similar across the tested settings.

Figure 8(a) varies KK under any-correct aggregation, with M-F1 ranging from 0.78 to 0.82. Figure 8(b) fixes K=5K=5 and varies the required number of correct answers. All tested thresholds remain effective, with the three-correct rule reaching M-F1 of 0.83. Overall, performance does not depend narrowly on a particular sample count or aggregation threshold.

Because these thresholds define different capability targets, we also compare the policies under a common single-attempt evaluation protocol. Each query receives a capability label based on one task answer from the corresponding trained model, and results are averaged over five trials. Figure 8(c) shows that the policies remain effective under this protocol. Overall, performance is broadly similar across the tested thresholds, supporting robustness to the aggregation threshold.

D.2.2 Diversity-Filtered Warm-up

Table 13 confirms the importance of DFW: without it, the policy collapses to almost always predicting Self-SOLVE (441/490 at 4B and 484/490 at 8B), and both M-F1 and CDS drop substantially. The reward standard deviation also falls sharply, showing that the rollout reward is too uniform to drive meaningful policy updates without DFW.

Beyond this ablation, we find that stronger models yield smaller diversified subsets and that rollout diversity emerges primarily on queries the model should delegate. We examine both patterns next.

Two findings on the diversified subset.

Finding 1: Stronger models yield smaller diversified subsets. Figure 10 shows the number of Math queries that pass the diversification filter as a function of model size. The subset shrinks sharply with scale: the 1.7B policy contributes roughly 550 diversified samples, and the 4B/8B/14B policies all fall below 200. This is consistent with the diversification criterion acting as an uncertainty filter: as the policy becomes stronger, its 16 rollouts on a given query are more likely to agree (all Self-Solve or all Delegate), and fewer queries survive the “both labels present” condition. Larger models are simply more internally consistent about what they can and cannot do, and the per-step cost of DFW decreases naturally with scale.

Finding 2: Rollout diversity emerges primarily on queries the model should delegate. Figure 10 contrasts the label distribution of the diversified subset (solid) against the full training set (hatched). The comparison against the full set is what makes this finding meaningful: since the diversified subset is by construction a subset of the full training data, if the model had no preference about which queries trigger rollout disagreement, the Self-Solve / Delegate proportions in the two distributions should roughly match. Instead, we observe a clear and systematic shift—across all four model sizes, the diversified subset is skewed toward Delegate (62%–70%), compared to a 20%–34% Delegate rate in the full data. This shift indicates that rollout diversity does not arise uniformly across the data, but emerges preferentially on queries that lie beyond the model’s reliable solving capability. On clearly-within- and clearly-beyond-capability queries the model’s 16 rollouts tend to agree. The boundary cases—where the model should delegate but is occasionally tempted to attempt—are exactly what surface in the diversified subset, and exactly where DFW’s training signal is most needed.

D.2.3 CSA Output Order

Because the models are autoregressive, the position of the <decision> tag determines how soon a routing decision is available. Under analysis-first the decision is emitted only after the rationale, a median of 8181–384384 tokens into the response depending on model and task. Under decision-first, inference can stop once the decision field is decoded, so routing requires only the prompt and decision tokens. Table 14 tests this change on three settings: decision-first CDS differs from analysis-first by 0.05, 1.41, and 0.05, respectively, while M-F1 is lower by 0.3–4.7 percentage points, computed before rounding the displayed means. These checkpoints were trained with analysis preceding the decision, so decision-first prompting also changes their expected output format. Across three random seeds, the standard deviation never exceeds 0.8 percentage points in M-F1 or accuracy and 0.510.51 in CDS.

D.3 Training Dynamics of SFT and RLVR

As shown in Figure 11, we track Qwen3-4B over three training epochs on Science, and the two methods exhibit sharply different trends. For SFTLabel, M-F1 against the original labels keeps rising while M-F1 against the re-probed labels drops, and problem-solving accuracy collapses sharply after the first epoch. Thus, the model learns a fixed delegation rule frozen at the base-model snapshot while its underlying capability changes. For RLVR, the two M-F1 curves rise together and problem-solving accuracy stays at the base level, indicating that self-assessment remains aligned with the model’s current capability. This contrast supports the assumption in Section 3.1: acquiring CSA should not come at the cost of the underlying problem-solving ability.

D.4 Capability-Preserving Training Baselines

Experimental settings are given in Appendix C.3. Table 15 provides the full mean ±\pm standard deviation results for the supervised baselines summarized in Table 3. The results separate two effects that are confounded in standard SFT: learning the CSA decision and preserving the solver whose capability is being assessed. These results are averaged across three runs; Table 2 reports the main training comparison.

SFT with smaller lr improves Macro-F1 over the Base model, but can substantially alter the underlying solver. This effect is most pronounced for Qwen3-1.7B, where CR falls to 72.472.4 on Math and 84.584.5 on Science. Qwen3-4B is more robust on Math (97.397.3 CR), but still loses substantial capability on Science (88.688.6). Thus, improved CSA accuracy under SFT with smaller lr does not necessarily correspond to faithful self-assessment of the original capability boundary.

LoRA SFT largely removes this failure mode: CR remains approximately 9999–100%100\% in all four settings. However, preserving capability alone is not sufficient to obtain consistently strong CSA. LoRA reaches a relatively high M-F1 of 0.730.73 for Qwen3-1.7B on Math, but drops to 0.510.51 on Science. For Qwen3-4B, it obtains 0.620.62 and 0.540.54 on Math and Science, respectively. The relatively large variation for some LoRA settings, such as 0.73±0.070.73\pm 0.07 on Qwen3-1.7B Math, also indicates greater run-to-run sensitivity than RLVR in these experiments.

KL-regularized SFT provides an intermediate trade-off. Relative to SFT with smaller lr, it generally improves capability retention—for example, from 72.472.4 to 90.690.6 CR on Qwen3-1.7B Math and from 84.584.5 to 92.092.0 on Science—but its CSA performance remains below RLVR. Task-mixed SFT similarly reduces capability degradation in several settings and performs strongly on Qwen3-4B Math, reaching 0.750.75 M-F1 with 100.2100.2 CR. However, its behavior is not uniform across domains: on Qwen3-1.7B Science, capability falls to 82.0±3.082.0\pm 3.0 despite mixing task-solving supervision into training.

In comparison, RLVR achieves the highest M-F1 in every model–domain setting: 0.840.84 and 0.660.66 for Qwen3-1.7B on Math and Science, and 0.850.85 and 0.670.67 for Qwen3-4B. At the same time, its CR remains close to or above the Base model in every case (100.3100.3–102.8%102.8\%). The standard deviations are also small for M-F1 (0.010.01–0.020.02 across the four settings). Taken together, these results indicate that RLVR’s advantage over supervised training is not merely due to the severe capability loss of naive SFT: the same pattern persists against LoRA, KL regularization, and task-mixed training, which explicitly or implicitly constrain changes to the base solver. RLVR preserves solving ability and beats DFW-matched SFT, suggesting that neither retention nor DFW’s training curriculum alone explains its gains. See Chu et al. (2025) and Shenfeld et al. (2026) for related discussions.

D.5 Training-Free Baselines

We describe the baselines in the order used in Table 16, grouped by the task outputs available when making the assessment. Baseline references are included in the table.

Query-based baselines.

These methods assess a query before generating a task answer. RLVR is the trained reference: it generates a CSA rationale and a binary decision. The remaining methods do not update model parameters. We describe the implemented scoring rules below, retaining the method names used in Table 16.

Internal confidence. We prompt the model to indicate whether it can answer correctly using Yes or No, without solving the problem. At each of the last six prompt positions, we apply the model’s output head to each returned hidden state, including the embedding state and transformer-layer states. We normalize the Yes and No logits to obtain qt,l=exp⁡(zt,lYes)/[exp⁡(zt,lYes)+exp⁡(zt,lNo)]q_{t,l}=\exp(z^{\mathrm{Yes}}_{t,l})/[\exp(z^{\mathrm{Yes}}_{t,l})+\exp(z^{\mathrm{No}}_{t,l})]. Internal confidence averages these values with normalized Gaussian weights that favor the final token and final layer. With locality parameter 1, the unnormalized weight is exp⁡[−(T−t)2−(L−l)2]\exp[-(T-t)^{2}-(L-l)^{2}]. No Yes/No response needs to be generated.

P(Yes). This uses only qT,Lq_{T,L}, the normalized Yes probability at the final prompt position and final layer. It measures the model’s explicit pre-answer judgment of its own ability.

P(Yes)-Mean. This takes the uniform mean of qt,lq_{t,l} over the last six prompt positions and all returned hidden states. Unlike internal confidence, it does not emphasize later positions or layers.

The next four scores use the likelihood of the input question itself, with answer options appended for Science. Let ℓt=log⁡p⁡(xt∣x<t)\ell_{t}=\log p(x_{t}\mid x_{<t}) for input tokens after the first. The implementation floors probabilities at 10−810^{-8} and orients all scores so that larger values indicate greater confidence.

Max token surprisal. We measure uncertainty using the largest input-token surprisal, maxt⁡(−ℓt)\max_{t}(-\ell_{t}). The confidence score is its negative, −maxt⁡(−ℓt)=mint⁡ℓt-\max_{t}(-\ell_{t})=\min_{t}\ell_{t}, so larger scores indicate greater confidence. This tests whether any input token is particularly unexpected to the model.

Predictive entropy. The implemented score is ∑tℓt\sum_{t}\ell_{t}, the negative total surprisal of the observed question. This is an input-likelihood score, not a full-vocabulary entropy calculation, and it is sensitive to question length.

Min-K. We select the five input tokens with the lowest log probabilities, or all available scored tokens if fewer than five exist. The score is the negative perplexity of this subset, −exp⁡[−meant∈I5⁡ℓt]-\exp[-\operatorname{mean}_{t\in I_{5}}\ell_{t}]. Here the five-token subset is unrelated to the number of sampled task answers used to construct capability labels.

Perplexity. We use negative question perplexity, −exp⁡[−meant⁡ℓt]-\exp[-\operatorname{mean}_{t}\ell_{t}]. Unlike Min-K, this averages over all scored input tokens; unlike the predictive-entropy score above, it normalizes by input length.

Single-answer-based baselines.

These methods generate one task answer before assessing it. Let a1,…,ama_{1},\ldots,a_{m} denote the generated solution tokens.

Sequence log-probability. The confidence score is the geometric mean of the generated tokens’ conditional probabilities, exp⁡[m−1​∑jlog⁡p⁡(aj∣x,a<j)]\exp[m^{-1}\sum_{j}\log p(a_{j}\mid x,a_{<j})]. This measures average likelihood of the sampled solution rather than its verified correctness.

Minimum token probability. The score is minj⁡p⁡(aj∣x,a<j)\min_{j}p(a_{j}\mid x,a_{<j}). It treats the least likely generated token as a signal of uncertainty, in contrast to averaging likelihood over the entire solution.

P(True). After producing a solution, the model receives the question and candidate answer and judges whether the answer is correct. The probability assigned to the affirmative judgment is used as confidence. This assesses a particular generated answer, whereas P(Yes) above asks about capability before an answer is available.

Verbalized confidence. The model is prompted to provide an answer together with a numerical probability that it is correct. We parse the stated probability and use it as the score, rather than reading confidence directly from token likelihoods.

Answer probability. We suppress reasoning and score the answer to which the model directly commits. For Science, the score is the largest option-letter probability after normalization over valid choices. For Math, it is the length-normalized likelihood of the directly generated answer span. It therefore excludes the likelihood of a full reasoning trace.

Multi-answer-based baselines.

Both methods use K=3,5,10K=3,5,10 independently sampled task solutions. Here KK controls the evidence available to the assessment method.

Self-consistency. We extract a final answer from each solution and use the number of votes for the most frequent valid answer divided by KK. Greater agreement yields higher confidence. Unparseable generations remain in the denominator but do not count as valid votes.

Semantic entropy. We group the same samples by final-answer equivalence, using exact-match answer strings for Math and option letters for Science. With empirical cluster proportions fjf_{j}, we compute H=−∑jfjlogfjH=-\sum_{j}f_{j}\log f_{j} and use 1−H/log⁡K1-H/\log K as confidence. Concentrated answers give high confidence; dispersed answers give low confidence. Unparseable generations form an additional cluster. This implementation uses answer equivalence rather than an entailment model, and agreement among unparseable outputs can inflate its score.

Simple reference strategies.

Always SELF-SOLVE assigns every query to the local model, while Always DELEGATE assigns every query to delegation. They show how the label distribution affects constant-decision Macro-F1. Random @ matched SSR assigns decisions randomly at the target self-solve rate, providing a reference that matches decision frequency without using query information.

Evaluation setting.

Figure 3 reports Qwen3-4B Math. Table 16 reports all four model-domain settings, including K=3,5,10K=3,5,10 for self-consistency and semantic entropy. Figure 3 uses the K=5K=5 results and reports M-F1 as a percentage. Solutions use temperature 1.0, top-pp 1.0, no top-kk truncation, and a maximum length of 4096 tokens. The auxiliary read-outs disable thinking. Direct-answer and verbalized-confidence generations use greedy decoding with maximum lengths of 64 and 128 tokens, respectively.

Labels and thresholds.

Training-free baselines are evaluated against the base model’s capability labels, and RLVR is evaluated against its own post-training labels. Query-based and single-answer-based baselines and simple strategies use the K=5K=5 evaluation labels. For each model, domain, method, and KK, we select the threshold that maximizes Macro-F1 on 500 calibration questions sampled from the training split with seed 42. Calibration questions are deduplicated and exclude all test questions. The selected threshold is then applied unchanged to the test set. The random reference’s self-solve rate is also set from calibration labels. Unresolved read-outs receive DELEGATE decisions. Unavailable CDS results are marked with a dash.

D.6 CSA Inference Efficiency

Table 17 shows that CSA assessments are fast in the measured settings: mean latency ranges from 0.39 to 1.32 seconds per query across four Qwen3 scales and two domains, with all Math settings below one second. We measure inference using vLLM on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU with batch size 1. Each query produces one non-thinking CSA response, with prefix caching disabled. Time is the mean wall-clock duration of generation requests after warm-up and excludes model loading and subsequent task solving. Generated-token counts come directly from vLLM token IDs and exclude prompt tokens.

D.7 Query-Level Capability Stability

Capability Ratio measures aggregate problem-solving performance, but it can conceal changes in which individual queries a model can solve. For example, CSA training could improve performance on some queries while degrading it on others, leaving average accuracy unchanged. We therefore evaluate whether CSA training changes the model’s query-level capability boundary.

Evaluation setting.

The analysis covers eight model–evaluation–policy settings formed by two evaluation domains (mathematics and code), two model sizes (Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B), and two CSA policies for each model (one trained on mathematics and one trained on science). The column “CSA policy” in Table 18 denotes the domain used to train the CSA policy, while “Evaluation” denotes the domain on which problem-solving capability is measured. For example, “Code / Qwen3-1.7B / Math” evaluates the coding capability of Qwen3-1.7B after CSA training on mathematics.

The mathematics evaluation contains 490490 queries and contributes 4×490=1,9604\times 490=1{,}960 query–policy pairs. The coding evaluation contains 722722 queries and contributes 4×722=2,8884\times 722=2{,}888 pairs. The complete analysis therefore contains 4,8484{,}848 query–policy pairs.

For each setting, we compare the original base checkpoint with the corresponding CSA-trained checkpoint. Both checkpoints use the same solving prompt, sampling parameters, answer parser, and correctness criterion. A mathematics response is correct when its extracted final answer matches the reference answer. A coding response is correct when the generated program passes the benchmark’s unit tests.

Capability labels and high-sample probes.

We construct the reported query-level capability labels from K=5K=5 independent solution attempts per query and checkpoint. Under the any-correct rule, a query receives the label Self-Solve if at least one of the five attempts is correct and receives Delegate otherwise.

Because a binary label constructed from five stochastic attempts is itself noisy, we additionally collect K=32K=32 attempts per query for both the base and CSA-trained checkpoints. These high-sample probes are used to estimate the label disagreement expected from finite sampling and to test for changes in each query’s underlying success probability. They are not used to redefine the reported K=5K=5 capability labels.

Capability-label churn.

Let yqbasey_{q}^{\mathrm{base}} and yqCSAy_{q}^{\mathrm{CSA}} denote the K=5K=5 capability labels assigned to query qq by the base and CSA-trained checkpoints. For an evaluation set containing NN queries, we define capability-label churn as

Churn=1N∑q=1N𝟏[yqbase≠yqCSA].\mathrm{Churn}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{q=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\left[y_{q}^{\mathrm{base}}\neq y_{q}^{\mathrm{CSA}}\right]. (9)

Churn is the fraction of queries that cross the binary capability boundary after CSA training. For example, a churn value of 0.050.05 means that the pre- and post-training labels differ on 5%5\% of the evaluation queries. Nonzero churn does not necessarily imply that the underlying capability changed, because two finite stochastic probes of the same checkpoint can produce different labels.

Cohen’s κ\kappa.

We complement churn with Cohen’s κ\kappa, which measures agreement between the base and CSA-trained labels after accounting for agreement expected from their overall label frequencies. Let

po=1−Churnp_{o}=1-\mathrm{Churn}

be the observed fraction of queries on which the two checkpoints agree. Let sbases_{\mathrm{base}} and sCSAs_{\mathrm{CSA}} denote the fractions of queries labeled Self-Solve by the base and CSA-trained checkpoints, respectively. The agreement expected from these marginal label frequencies is

pe=sbase​sCSA+(1−sbase)​(1−sCSA).p_{e}=s_{\mathrm{base}}s_{\mathrm{CSA}}+(1-s_{\mathrm{base}})(1-s_{\mathrm{CSA}}). (10)

Cohen’s κ\kappa is

κ=po−pe1−pe.\kappa=\frac{p_{o}-p_{e}}{1-p_{e}}. (11)

A value of κ=1\kappa=1 denotes perfect agreement. A value of κ=0\kappa=0 means that the observed agreement equals the agreement expected from the two checkpoints’ marginal label frequencies. This correction is useful when one label is common: if both checkpoints label almost every query Self-Solve, their raw agreement can be high even when it contains little query-specific information. In our experiments, mean raw agreement is 95.5%95.5\% and mean κ\kappa is 0.8950.895, showing that the base and CSA-trained checkpoints have highly similar query-level capability labels even after accounting for their overall label distributions.

Capability Ratio.

We also report Capability Ratio (CR) to measure aggregate capability preservation:

CR=AccCSAAccbase×100%,\mathrm{CR}=\frac{\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{CSA}}}{\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{base}}}\times 100\%, (12)

where Accbase\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{base}} and AccCSA\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{CSA}} are the problem-solving accuracies of the two checkpoints under the same evaluation protocol. Churn and κ\kappa measure query-level stability, whereas CR measures aggregate performance retention.

Finite-sampling null.

The K=5K=5 capability label can change across repeated probes even when the underlying checkpoint is unchanged. We estimate this finite-sampling variability using the K=32K=32 probe of the base checkpoint.

For query qq, let cqc_{q} be the number of correct responses among the 3232 base-checkpoint attempts. Under the any-correct rule, the probability that a random subset of five attempts receives a Self-Solve label is

πq=1−(32−cq5)(325).\pi_{q}=1-\frac{\binom{32-c_{q}}{5}}{\binom{32}{5}}. (13)

The probability that two independently sampled K=5K=5 labels disagree is then

νq=2​πq​(1−πq).\nu_{q}=2\pi_{q}(1-\pi_{q}). (14)

We define the sampling-noise null for an evaluation cell as

Null=1N​∑q=1Nνq,\mathrm{Null}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{q=1}^{N}\nu_{q}, (15)

and define excess churn as

Excess=Churn−Null.\mathrm{Excess}=\mathrm{Churn}-\mathrm{Null}. (16)

Positive excess churn indicates more pre/post label disagreement than expected from finite sampling alone. Excess churn near or below zero indicates that the observed disagreement is comparable to the variability of repeated K=5K=5 measurements.

Bootstrap uncertainty.

We estimate uncertainty in excess churn using a paired bootstrap over queries. Within each evaluation cell, we sample NN queries with replacement and recompute both observed churn and the sampling-noise null on the same resampled queries. We record their difference for each of 20002000 bootstrap replicates and use the 2.52.5th and 97.597.5th percentiles of the resulting distribution as the paired-bootstrap 95%95\% confidence interval.

Aggregate stability results.

Table 18 shows that query-level capability remains stable within the resolution of our evaluation. Across the eight settings, mean observed label churn is 4.5%4.5\%, compared with 5.4%5.4\% disagreement expected from finite sampling. Mean excess churn is therefore −0.9-0.9 percentage points. No evaluation cell has a statistically positive excess over its sampling-noise null. Agreement between the pre- and post-training labels also remains high, with mean κ=0.895\kappa=0.895, while the mean Capability Ratio is 101.0%101.0\%.

Per-query changes in success probability.

Label churn measures changes in a thresholded K=5K=5 capability label. We additionally test whether CSA training changes each query’s underlying success probability using the K=32K=32 high-sample probes.

For each query–policy pair, we construct the following 2×22\times 2 contingency table:

CorrectIncorrectBasecqbase32−cqbaseCSAcqCSA32−cqCSA.\begin{array}[]{c|cc}&\mathrm{Correct}&\mathrm{Incorrect}\\ \hline\cr\mathrm{Base}&c_{q}^{\mathrm{base}}&32-c_{q}^{\mathrm{base}}\\ \mathrm{CSA}&c_{q}^{\mathrm{CSA}}&32-c_{q}^{\mathrm{CSA}}.\end{array} (17)

We apply a two-sided Fisher exact test to each of the 4,8484{,}848 query–policy pairs and control the false discovery rate at 0.050.05 using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure across the complete family of tests.

Only 3232 of the 4,8484{,}848 comparisons (0.66%0.66\%) are identified as changes after correction. All 3232 occur in the coding evaluation: 33 and 77 for the two Qwen3-1.7B policies, and 1111 for each Qwen3-4B policy. None of the 1,9601{,}960 mathematics comparisons is identified as a change.

Measurement resolution and limitations.

The churn and κ\kappa analyses concern the binary capability labels induced by the specified K=5K=5 aggregation rule. They do not establish that the checkpoints have identical continuous success probabilities on every query. Likewise, a per-query comparison that is not rejected should not be interpreted as proof that the two success probabilities are equal. With 3232 attempts per checkpoint, small changes may remain unresolved.

Each evaluation cell contains approximately 500500 to 700700 queries. At this sample size, the paired-bootstrap confidence intervals rule out aggregate excess label churn larger than approximately 22–33 percentage points. Our conclusion is therefore that CSA training preserves the model’s query-level capability boundary within the resolution of this evaluation.

D.8 Within-Source Discrimination on Math

Figure 6 tests whether Math CSA decisions identify solvable queries beyond benchmark source identity. We evaluate the six Math-trained RLVR models from Table 2 on the same 490 questions: 300 GSM8K, 100 MATH500, and 90 AIME. Each decision is matched to the same query’s post-training capability label, constructed by any-correct aggregation over five task attempts. We exclude invalid decisions: three for OLMo2-13B and none for the other models.

For each model, we hold the capability labels fixed and independently permute the binary decisions within each source. Every permutation preserves that model’s exact numbers of Self-SOLVE and DELEGATE decisions in each source. Thus, a preference for delegating AIME is preserved, while any association between a decision and the particular query’s solvability within AIME is removed. We compute pooled Macro-F1 across the three sources after each permutation, rather than averaging three source-specific F1 scores.

We generate B=100,000B=100{,}000 null draws with random seed 20260924. The implementation samples the number of true positives within each source from its conditional hypergeometric distribution, which is equivalent to uniformly shuffling binary decisions while fixing their counts. The blue markers in Figure 6 show the null mean; the bars show its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. Orange markers show the observed score, and annotations give its improvement over the null mean in percentage points. These bars describe the permutation null, not confidence intervals for the observed score. A one-sided Monte Carlo pp-value is (1+#{M−F1b≥M−F1obs})/(B+1)(1+\#\{M-F1_{b}\geq M-F1_{\mathrm{obs}}\})/(B+1). The saved analysis applies Holm correction jointly to the six Math tests and an additional exploratory Omni-MATH test; all six Math results remain below 0.0020.002 under this seven-test correction.

Table 19 reports the numerical values underlying Figure 6. Observed Macro-F1 exceeds the source-preserving null by 3.44–9.61 percentage points. Source-dependent routing frequencies alone therefore do not explain the observed performance. This pooled test demonstrates discrimination within sources overall; it does not imply equally strong discrimination in every individual source.

D.9 Zero-Shot Transfer to Coding

We test whether CSA learned from math or science transfers to Python programming without further training. Our evaluation contains 722 problems from HumanEval+ (Chen et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023), MBPP+ (Austin et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023), and a LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025) subset with organizer-provided difficulty labels. To reduce contamination risk, we include only LiveCodeBench contests held after the models’ reported pretraining cutoff. We assess solution correctness by running each generated program against the benchmark’s unit tests in a sandbox. Both trained policies are compared with the base model using the same CSA prompt. We also measure each checkpoint’s coding ability separately, so its assessment decisions are evaluated against its own post-training performance.

Transfer performance and capability retention.

As shown in Table 20, CSA training improves coding assessment: Macro-F1 rises from 0.36 to 0.64 for the 1.7B model and from 0.41 to 0.63 for the 4B model, with similar gains from math and science training. The transferred policies choose Self-SOLVE on 95–99% of easy problems, but only 11–33% of hard problems. The prompted base models, by comparison, delegate at most two of the 722 problems, even though they solve fewer than 17% of hard problems. These assessment gains accompany Capability Ratios of 100–103%, indicating that overall coding ability is retained. Formatting failures are also rare, occurring in only 0.5–1.1% of attempts.

Does the policy identify which problems to delegate?

An increase in Macro-F1 could result simply from delegating more often. To test whether the policies identify the right problems to delegate, we randomly shuffle each policy’s decisions across problems within sources. This preserves the number of Self-SOLVE and DELEGATE decisions but removes their association with individual problems. As shown in Table 20, the policies’ observed Macro-F1 scores are 7.8–10.6 standard deviations above this shuffled baseline (p<0.001p<0.001). Thus, their gains reflect an ability to distinguish solvable from unsolvable problems beyond what a change in delegation frequency alone would achieve. This provides evidence that CSA transfers to coding, a domain not included in CSA training.

Reporting CDS.

We omit CDS for the base models because they delegate only one or two problems. Such small delegation groups make the statistic unstable and unsuitable for comparison.

D.10 CSA Is Model Specific

To test whether CSA teaches a signal specific to the model carrying it, we compared each Qwen policy against OLMoE-1B-7B (Muennighoff et al., 2025), from a different lab with a different training corpus. We measured per-problem competence for both the policy’s own model and OLMoE by sampling 32 solutions each on the same 722 coding problems and running the unit tests, so both sides are estimated with identical precision. The question is then whether a policy’s decisions follow its own model’s measured success rate or CSA is just tracking problem difficulty.

All four policies follow their own model as shown in Table 22. The partial correlation with own competence is consistently stronger than the correlation with OLMoE’s, and every bootstrap confidence interval excludes zero, with effects ranging from +0.157 to +0.258. Table 23 gives the same conclusion in operational terms: delegating the problems OLMoE is least likely to solve (using 32 executed samples per problem) is a worse policy than what CSA produces from the problem text alone, in all four cells. CSA also discriminates among problems that OLMoE rates as equally hard (residual-null z of 3.79 to 5.44). Two checks rule out the obvious artifacts: the competence estimates are near-equally reliable (split-half 0.985 / 0.990 / 0.958), and OLMoE’s pass rates correlate substantially with the Qwen models’ (r = 0.666 and 0.528), so it is a relevant comparator rather than a noisy or irrelevant one.

Table 24 examines aggregate alignment when each of three CSA policies is paired with each solver. Policy coverage increases with the size of the model it was trained for (0.785, 0.891, and 0.892). Pairing the 8B policy with the 1.7B solver yields a coverage–accuracy gap of approximately 11 percentage points. Matched pairings have a smaller mean absolute coverage–accuracy gap than mismatched pairings (0.049 versus 0.072). The 1.7B matched pair has a gap of +0.003, while the 4B and 8B policies have nearly identical coverage. This aggregate comparison is suggestive and does not establish query-level model specificity on its own.

Figure 12 further shows that RLVR decisions adapt to model capability: weaker models DELEGATE more, while stronger models Self-SOLVE more.

D.11 Case Studies

To illustrate concretely how RLVR shapes CSA, we present case studies in Math and Science.

Math Problem

As shown in Figure 13, we provide the complete reasoning traces for the math case study. The Vanilla Qwen3-4B model confidently chooses to Self-SOLVE, but produces an incorrect answer across all five sampled responses. In contrast, the RLVR-trained model recognizes that the problem is beyond its reliable capability and chooses to DELEGATE. This example illustrates how RLVR teaches the model to recognize when a query exceeds its competence.

Science Problem

Figure 14 presents an additional case study on a science question, where the same pattern emerges: the vanilla model answers confidently but incorrectly, while the RLVR-trained model recognizes its uncertainty and delegates.

D.12 Applications of CSA

D.12.1 Self-Routing

We provide illustrative figures for self-routing in Figure 15. Formally, given a query xx, the local model first produces a CSA decision y^=ℳlocalCSA​(x)∈{Self-SOLVE,DELEGATE}\hat{y}=\mathcal{M}_{\text{local}}^{\text{CSA}}(x)\in\{\textsc{Self-SOLVE},\textsc{DELEGATE}\}, and the routed answer is

a^​(x)={ℳlocal​(x),y^=Self-SOLVE,ℳcloud​(x),y^=DELEGATE.\hat{a}(x)=\begin{cases}\mathcal{M}_{\text{local}}(x),&\hat{y}=\textsc{Self-SOLVE},\\ \mathcal{M}_{\text{cloud}}(x),&\hat{y}=\textsc{DELEGATE}.\end{cases} (18)

This setup exposes a direct cost–accuracy trade-off between the two extremes of local-only inference (cheap but limited by the local model’s capability) and cloud-only inference (accurate but expensive on every query). An ideal CSA policy delegates exactly the queries the local model cannot solve, approaching cloud-only accuracy at a fraction of the cost.

Random routing at a matched cloud-call budget.

For the Math routing comparison in Table 8, random routing selects a uniformly random subset of exactly mm out of N=490N=490 queries for cloud inference and answers the rest locally. We set mm to the corresponding CSA policy’s cloud-call count: 96 for Qwen3-1.7B and 73 for Qwen3-4B. Let Li,Ci∈{0,1}L_{i},C_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicate correctness of the stored single local and cloud answers to query ii. The exact expected accuracy over random subsets is

𝔼⁡[Accrandom]=1N​∑i=1N[(1−ρ)​Li+ρ​Ci],ρ=mN.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Acc}_{\mathrm{random}}]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[(1-\rho)L_{i}+\rho C_{i}\right],\qquad\rho=\frac{m}{N}. (19)

We use the same stored branch outputs to evaluate CSA and random routing. The expected random-routing accuracies are 0.6504 and 0.7182, compared with CSA accuracies of 0.7327 and 0.8000. These are exact expectations conditional on the recorded answers, not estimates from a single random subset. The comparison isolates query selection at the same cloud-call budget. The time and token measurements in Table 8 come from a separate generation run of each CSA model at batch size 1. They measure assessment overhead, excluding local and cloud answer generation. The routing accuracies and cloud-call counts come from the stored routing evaluation.

D.12.2 Cost-Aware Routing as an Extension of RLVR-Trained CSA

Matching the single-attempt deployment setting.

The Math any-correct label measures whether a model succeeds in at least one of five attempts. It does not represent single-attempt success: under independent attempts, a query with success probability 0.20.2 receives a Self-SOLVE label with probability 1−(1−0.2)5≈0.671-(1-0.2)^{5}\approx 0.67. A deployed router that obtains only one answer from the selected solver instead benefits from predicting each action’s expected outcome. The experiment below addresses this practical setting using an expected-outcome reward. Five sampled answers estimate each branch’s single-call success probability. Evaluation averages these outcomes under the same routing protocol for every method, without selecting the best of five answers. We keep the local and cloud solvers fixed so that policy comparisons use the same branch outcomes.

From capability assessment to routing utility.

The CSA policy decides whether a model should attempt a query or seek help. We extend this policy to a local–cloud setting in which the selected action is evaluated by the answer it produces and delegation incurs a cost (Chen et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025; Aggarwal et al., 2024). The action space, assessment prompt, and RLVR training framework remain unchanged, and only the reward is replaced by downstream routing utility. For a query qq, let pL​(q)p_{\mathrm{L}}(q) and pC​(q)p_{\mathrm{C}}(q) denote the probabilities that the local and cloud models answer correctly. The utility of action aa is

{pL​(q),a=Self-SOLVE,pC​(q)−λ​C,a=DELEGATE,\begin{cases}p_{\mathrm{L}}(q),&a=\textsc{Self-SOLVE},\\ p_{\mathrm{C}}(q)-\lambda C,&a=\textsc{DELEGATE},\end{cases} (20)

where CC is the cost of a cloud call and λ\lambda controls the cost–accuracy trade-off. The corresponding oracle delegates exactly when

pC​(q)−pL​(q)>λ​C.p_{\mathrm{C}}(q)-p_{\mathrm{L}}(q)>\lambda C. (21)

This objective generalizes the original CSA decision. If local capability is binary, delegation always succeeds, and delegation is free, Eq. (20) recovers the rule of delegating precisely when the local model cannot solve the query. In the more realistic setting, delegation is rewarded only when its expected improvement exceeds its cost.

Models and datasets.

We use Qwen3-1.7B as the local model and Qwen3-32B as the cloud model. We evaluate on the same Science domain as in the main experiments, comprising the biology, chemistry, health, and physics categories of MMLU-Pro with 3,266 training and 700 test queries. We set C=1C=1, so λ\lambda directly represents the penalty assigned to one cloud call.

Estimating action outcomes.

For each query, we sample K=5K=5 answers independently from both the local and cloud models and compute empirical single-call success rates

1K∑k=1K𝟏[a^m(k)(q)=a∗(q)],m∈L,C.\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{1}\left[\hat{a}_{m}^{(k)}(q)=a^{*}(q)\right],\qquad m\in{\mathrm{L},\mathrm{C}}. (22)

We use these pass rates in Eq. (20).

For each value of λ\lambda, we apply the same two-stage RLVR procedure used for CSA. Diversity-Filtered Warm-up first retains training queries whose 16 policy rollouts contain both actions. Training then continues on the full distribution. GRPO uses 16 rollouts per prompt, a global batch size of 64, one epoch, a learning rate of 10−610^{-6}, a KL coefficient of 0.010.01, and full-parameter optimization with ZeRO-3 on four NVIDIA L40S GPUs. During training, we use the empirical expected-outcome reward

{p^L​(q),a=Self-SOLVE,p^C​(q)−λ​C,a=DELEGATE.\begin{cases}\hat{p}_{\mathrm{L}}(q),&a=\textsc{Self-SOLVE},\\ \hat{p}_{\mathrm{C}}(q)-\lambda C,&a=\textsc{DELEGATE}.\end{cases} (23)

This is the expectation of a sampled correctness reward under the empirical branch outcomes. Using the expectation removes within-action sampling variance, so the GRPO advantage reflects the quality of the routing decision. Unparseable policy outputs receive a reward of −1-1, below the reward of either valid action.

Cost grid.

Because K=5K=5, each empirical success rate is quantized in increments of 0.20.2. We use

λ∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7},\lambda\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7\}, (24)

which places each cost between adjacent achievable outcome differences and avoids ties in Eq. (20). We train a separate policy for each value and report its realized delegation rate rather than assuming that the grid produces evenly spaced operating points.

Evaluation protocol.

We evaluate every routing policy using frozen copies of the local and cloud solvers. Freezing both branches keeps the outcome estimates stationary and ensures that differences between policies arise from which queries they delegate rather than changes in solving ability. Policy decisions are sampled at temperature 1.01.0 over three random seeds. Let dπ​(q)=1d_{\pi}(q)=1 when policy π\pi delegates and 00 otherwise. Its routed accuracy and delegation rate are

Acc⁡(π)\displaystyle\operatorname{Acc}(\pi) =1N​∑q[(1−dπ​(q))​p^L​(q)+dπ​(q)​p^C​(q)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{q}\left[\bigl(1-d_{\pi}(q)\bigr)\hat{p}_{\mathrm{L}}(q)+d_{\pi}(q)\hat{p}_{\mathrm{C}}(q)\right], (25)
ρ⁡(π)\displaystyle\rho(\pi) =1N​∑qdπ​(q).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{q}d_{\pi}(q). (26)

We report the resulting cost–accuracy frontier in Figure 16.

The figure shows that outcome-aware RLVR is the strongest deployable routing method for Qwen3-1.7B on science. The trained RLVR policies lie above the baseline cluster.

The two dashed curves clarify why outcome-aware training helps. The upper oracle knows the benefit of delegation, pcloud−plocalp_{\mathrm{cloud}}-p_{\mathrm{local}}, whereas the lower oracle knows only whether the local model will succeed. The local model fails on 49.1%49.1\% of queries, but the cloud model can rescue only 29.929.9 percentage points. On the remaining 19.219.2 points, both models fail. A capability-only signal cannot distinguish these cases and may therefore delegate queries for which a cloud call provides no benefit. By optimizing the outcomes of both actions, RLVR learns a substantially better routing policy.

The operating point still matters. With larger penalties, the policies converge to never delegating, partly because many training groups provide no decision-level learning signal. Nevertheless, the clear gains at matched delegation rates show that RLVR learns which queries benefit from cloud assistance substantially better than the available baselines.

D.12.3 Self-Guided Data Selection

Our main data-selection experiment tests whether examples preferred by an RLVR-trained CSA model are better fine-tuning data than examples selected by standard data-selection baselines. We begin with a base model M0M_{0} and train a CSA model MRLVRM_{\mathrm{RLVR}} to decide whether a problem should be answered directly or delegated. After training, the model is used as a scorer: it is applied to a fresh candidate training pool

𝒟pool={(xi,yi)}i=1N,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pool}}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, (27)

and assigns each candidate a delegation-derived score. Let ziselfz_{i}^{\mathrm{self}} and zidelz_{i}^{\mathrm{del}} denote the logits assigned by MRLVRM_{\mathrm{RLVR}} to the Self_Solve and Delegate decision tokens for example xix_{i}. We convert these logits into a normalized delegation probability

pidel=exp⁡(zidel)exp⁡(zidel)+exp⁡(ziself).p_{i}^{\mathrm{del}}=\frac{\exp(z_{i}^{\mathrm{del}})}{\exp(z_{i}^{\mathrm{del}})+\exp(z_{i}^{\mathrm{self}})}. (28)

Intuitively, pidelp_{i}^{\mathrm{del}} estimates how strongly the trained CSA policies believe that M0M_{0} should not solve xix_{i} directly.

A naive delegate-only selector would choose examples with the largest pidelp_{i}^{\mathrm{del}}. However, this can over-select extreme examples that are far beyond the model’s current capabilities or are noisy, ambiguous, or mismatched to the target distribution. To avoid this, we use a delegate-based loss-bandpass selector. First, we compute the base model’s supervised loss on each candidate:

ℓi=−1|yi|∑t=1|yi|logpM0(yi,t∣xi,yi,<t).\ell_{i}=-\frac{1}{|y_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_{i}|}\log p_{M_{0}}(y_{i,t}\mid x_{i},y_{i,<t}). (29)

We then retain only examples whose loss lies within a middle band:

ℬα,β={i:Qα​({ℓj}j=1N)≤ℓi≤Qβ​({ℓj}j=1N)},\mathcal{B}_{\alpha,\beta}=\left\{i:Q_{\alpha}(\{\ell_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N})\leq\ell_{i}\leq Q_{\beta}(\{\ell_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N})\right\}, (30)

where QαQ_{\alpha} and QβQ_{\beta} are empirical loss quantiles. This removes examples that are already too easy for M0M_{0} as well as extreme high-loss outliers. Among the remaining examples, we rank by delegation probability:

siDLB=pidel⋅𝟏{i∈ℬα,β}.s_{i}^{\mathrm{DLB}}=p_{i}^{\mathrm{del}}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{B}_{\alpha,\beta}\}. (31)

For a target selection budget kk, the selected subset is

𝒮DLB​(k)=TopKi∈{1,…,N}⁡(siDLB,k).\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{DLB}}(k)=\operatorname{TopK}_{i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}}\left(s_{i}^{\mathrm{DLB}},k\right). (32)

We then fine-tune the model on 𝒮DLB​(k)\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{DLB}}(k). Figure 17 provides an overview of the method.

For the science-pool experiments, we train M0M_{0} on MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024) to get MRLVRM_{\mathrm{RLVR}}. The candidate pool is MedMCQA (Pal et al., 2022). We randomly sample N=50,000N=50{,}000 examples from the MedMCQA training split and score them using our method and all baselines. We conduct experiments on Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025). We use loss-bandpass quantiles Qα=0.2,Qβ=0.8Q_{\alpha}=0.2,Q_{\beta}=0.8. We compare delegate-based loss-bandpass against random selection, high-loss selection, low-loss selection, and development-set similarity selection. We also include an all-samples condition, which fine-tunes on the full 50,000-example candidate pool. For development-set similarity, we reserve a held-out set

𝒟dev={(xjdev,yjdev)}j=1m\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{dev}}=\{(x_{j}^{\mathrm{dev}},y_{j}^{\mathrm{dev}})\}_{j=1}^{m} (33)

of m=500m=500 randomly selected MedMCQA training examples that are excluded from the candidate pool.

The baseline selectors are defined as follows. Random selection samples a subset uniformly without replacement:

𝒮rand​(k)∼Unif⁡({𝒮⊂𝒟pool:|𝒮|=k}).\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\sim\operatorname{Unif}\left(\{\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pool}}:|\mathcal{S}|=k\}\right). (34)

High-loss selection ranks examples by the base model loss in Eq. (29) and selects the largest-loss examples:

𝒮high​(k)=TopKi⁡(ℓi,k).\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{high}}(k)=\operatorname{TopK}_{i}\left(\ell_{i},k\right). (35)

This baseline tests whether our method is simply performing hard-example mining. Low-loss selection selects the examples with the smallest base-model loss:

𝒮low​(k)=TopKi⁡(−ℓi,k).\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{low}}(k)=\operatorname{TopK}_{i}\left(-\ell_{i},k\right). (36)

This baseline tests whether improvements can instead be obtained by emphasizing examples that are already easy and likely to be clean.

For development-set similarity, we embed each candidate xix_{i} and each development example xjdevx_{j}^{\mathrm{dev}} using a fixed sentence encoder f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot). We compute the maximum cosine similarity between each candidate and the held-out development set:

sisim=max1≤j≤m⁡f​(xi)⊤​f​(xjdev)‖f⁡(xi)‖2​‖f⁡(xjdev)‖2.s_{i}^{\mathrm{sim}}=\max_{1\leq j\leq m}\frac{f(x_{i})^{\top}f(x_{j}^{\mathrm{dev}})}{\|f(x_{i})\|_{2}\,\|f(x_{j}^{\mathrm{dev}})\|_{2}}. (37)

The selected subset is then

𝒮sim​(k)=TopKi⁡(sisim,k).\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{sim}}(k)=\operatorname{TopK}_{i}\left(s_{i}^{\mathrm{sim}},k\right). (38)

This baseline controls for the possibility that delegate-based selection works only because it selects examples similar to the evaluation distribution.

Finally, the all-samples condition uses

𝒮all=𝒟pool,\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{all}}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pool}}, (39)

and therefore measures the performance obtained when no data selection is performed. All selected subsets of size kk are fine-tuned using the same optimization hyperparameters, number of epochs, and training budget, so differences in downstream performance can be attributed to the selection rule rather than to changes in compute or training procedure.

Given the scored candidate pool, we run fixed-budget SFT experiments. For each selection method, we fine-tune on one of three budget fractions of the 50,000-example pool: 5%, 10%, and 20% corresponding to 2,500, 5,000, and 10,000 selected examples. Fine-tuning is performed with full-parameter training on NVIDIA L40S nodes. The main hyperparameters are a learning rate of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, per-device batch size 4, maximum sequence length 4096, maximum training steps 2000, and bfloat16 training. Evaluation is performed on the MedMCQA validation split rather than the official test split. Each run evaluates on 500 randomly sampled validation examples with a maximum generation length of 256 tokens. The evaluation set is identical for all methods. The primary metric is validation accuracy after fine-tuning.

Appendix E Prompt Templates

E.1 CSA Prompt Template

We use the following prompt template to elicit the model’s Self-Solve / Delegate decision on each query. The template instructs the model to assess its own capability, and to emit its decision in a structured format consisting of an <analysis> block followed by a <decision> block. The same template is used for all subsequent CSA inference throughout the paper.

We parse the model’s response by extracting the content of the <decision> block and matching it against Self-Solve or Delegate.

E.2 Self-Rationale Prompt (SFTSelf)

The training model itself is prompted to produce a self-assessment justifying the ground-truth label. The placeholders {query} and {decision} are replaced with the query qiq_{i} and the label yi∈{Self_Solve,Delegate}y_{i}\in\{\textsc{Self\_Solve},\textsc{Delegate}\}, respectively.

E.3 Teacher-Rationale Prompt (SFTTeacher)

A stronger teacher model ℳ∗\mathcal{M}^{*} is prompted to produce a rationale on behalf of the target model. The teacher is instructed to write in the first-person perspective of the target model so that the resulting rationale stylistically resembles a self-assessment, even though it is generated externally.
